lead: A modern car has tens of electronic control units (ECUs), and most of them need data that another ECU measures. Running one copper wire for every signal between every pair of units makes a harness that is heavy, costly and full of connectors that can fail. A data bus solves this: all the units share one pair of wires and send their data as short numbered messages. This chapter explains how data moves between automotive electronic systems, why one signal is used by many systems at once, and what a vehicle bus must guarantee before it can carry engine, brake or door data.
prereq: You need the vehicle power supply, wire sizing and circuit diagrams, and the idea of a sensor that gives an electrical signal.

sections.h3: Data transfer between ECUs: wires, signals and messages

blocks.text: An electronic control unit (ECU) is a small computer: a microcontroller with memory, input circuits for sensors, output drivers for actuators and a communication interface. A node is anything that sends or receives on a network; every ECU is a node, and so is the diagnostic socket when a scan tool is plugged in. A signal is one quantity, such as engine speed or a door-open switch. A message (or frame) is one packet on the bus; one message usually carries several signals packed side by side.

In the older point-to-point method, each signal has its own wire from the unit that measures it to every unit that uses it. If engine speed is needed by the instrument cluster, the gearbox ECU and the air-conditioning ECU, three wires carry the same value. With a serial data bus, the engine ECU puts engine speed into one message, sends it once, and every unit that needs it reads it. Sending many signals over one medium in turn is called multiplexing.

blocks.where: L is the number of links needed to join every one of n units directly to every other one. A bus needs one shared pair of wires and one transceiver (the transmit-receive circuit) per unit, so its cost grows only as n.

blocks.text: Inside one ECU, chips talk over short board-level links, which some syllabi call communication protocols in embedded systems: UART (start and stop bits; also the basis of LIN), SPI (a fast clocked link to memory or driver chips) and I²C (two wires shared by sensors). They work over centimetres; a vehicle bus must work over metres of harness, in electrical noise, between units from different suppliers.
A cross-system function is a vehicle feature that no single ECU can perform alone. It is the strongest reason for networking. Some everyday examples:

items: Traction control: the ABS ECU sees a driven wheel spinning faster than the others and sends a torque-reduction request; the engine ECU retards ignition or closes the throttle.
Wheel speed: measured once by the ABS ECU, it is used by the speedometer, the odometer, the navigation unit, the electric power steering (lighter steering at low speed) and the gearbox ECU.
Automatic gear shift: the gearbox ECU asks the engine ECU for a short torque dip during each shift, so the shift is smooth.
Crash unlock: the airbag ECU sends a crash message; the body ECU unlocks the doors and switches on the hazard lamps.

blocks.text: Car makers group ECUs into domains by the kind of data they exchange: powertrain (engine, gearbox), chassis (ABS, ESP, steering, suspension), body and comfort (doors, seats, lamps, climate), infotainment (radio, navigation, phone, displays) and diagnostics. Each domain has its own bus, chosen for its needs, and a gateway ECU joins the domains and forwards only the messages that must cross.
A vehicle bus is judged on a short list of requirements. The examiner expects you to name them and to say which systems need which.

items: Data rate (bandwidth): the bits per second the bus can carry, from about 20 kbit/s for a door module to 100 Mbit/s for a camera.
Latency: the delay from a unit deciding to send a value to the receiver having it, in milliseconds or microseconds.
Determinism: the worst-case delay is known and guaranteed, not just small on average. Brakes and steering need this; a seat motor does not.
Reliability: errors must be detected (check sums, acknowledgement) and a faulty node must not block the others.
Fault tolerance: some functions must keep working after a broken wire or a failed node.
EMC: the bus must not radiate interference and must survive ignition and motor noise.
Cost per node, sleep and wake-up: cheap enough for dozens of small units, and able to sleep in a parked car and wake on a message.
Expandability and diagnosis: new units can be added without rewiring, and a workshop tester can reach every unit.

blocks.text: Because the bus is shared, its time is a limited resource. The bus load U is the fraction of time the bus is busy:
U = (Σ bits per message ÷ period of that message) ÷ bit rate
blocks.where: the sum runs over every periodic message; bits per message is the frame length on the wire; the period is how often the message is sent (s); the bit rate is in bit/s. A common design target is to keep U below about 60 to 70 per cent, so that retries after errors and messages added later still fit.

examples.question: A car has 12 ECUs, and each must exchange data with every other ECU. (a) How many links does full point-to-point wiring need, and how many line driver circuits at the link ends? (b) How many transceivers does one shared bus need? (c) How many fewer driver circuits is that?
steps: Links for full point-to-point wiring: L = n(n − 1) / 2 = 12 × 11 / 2 = 132 / 2 = 66 links.
Each link has a driver at each end: 2L = 2 × 66 = 132 driver circuits.
A bus needs one transceiver per unit: 12 transceivers, on one shared twisted pair.
Saving: 132 − 12 = 120 driver circuits, and 66 separate cable runs become one.
examples.answer: Point-to-point wiring needs 66 links with 132 line drivers; one bus needs 12 transceivers, 120 fewer.

examples.question: A powertrain CAN bus runs at 500 kbit/s. Twenty messages are sent every 10 ms and eight more every 20 ms. Each message takes 125 bits on the wire. (a) Find the bus load. (b) Can four new messages of 125 bits every 10 ms be added if the load must stay under 70 per cent?
steps: Bits per second from the 10 ms group: 20 × 125 bits ÷ 0.010 s = 2500 ÷ 0.010 = 250 000 bit/s.
Bits per second from the 20 ms group: 8 × 125 bits ÷ 0.020 s = 1000 ÷ 0.020 = 50 000 bit/s.
Bus load: U = 300 000 ÷ 500 000 = 0.60, that is 60 per cent.
New messages: 4 × 125 ÷ 0.010 = 50 000 bit/s, so the demand becomes 350 000 bit/s.
New load: 350 000 ÷ 500 000 = 0.70, exactly 70 per cent, which is not under the limit.
examples.answer: The load is 60 per cent now; the four new messages would raise it to 70 per cent, so they do not fit under the 70 per cent limit. Send them every 20 ms (load 65 per cent) or move some messages to another bus.

traps: Counting each pair twice: 12 units need 66 point-to-point links, not 132. The 132 is the number of link ends.
A signal is not a message: one message usually carries several signals, so "one wire per signal" becomes "one message for several signals", not one message per signal.
High bandwidth is not determinism. A fast bus can still have an unknown worst-case delay if messages queue; determinism means the worst case is guaranteed.
Bus load uses the period of each message, not the number of messages alone: 20 messages every 10 ms load the bus twice as much as 20 messages every 20 ms.
A gateway is not a junction box: it is an ECU that decides which messages cross, and it can change their rate or format.

quiz.a: An ECU is a small computer that reads sensors and drives actuators. A node is any device that sends or receives on the network. A signal is one quantity, such as engine speed, carried inside a message.

quiz.q: List five requirements for a vehicle bus system.
quiz.a: Any five of: data rate, latency, determinism, error detection and reliability, fault tolerance, EMC, low cost per node, sleep and wake-up, expandability, diagnostic access.

quiz.q: What is a cross-system function? Give two examples.
quiz.a: A feature that needs data or actions from more than one ECU. Examples: traction control (ABS ECU asks the engine ECU to cut torque); crash unlock (airbag ECU tells the body ECU to unlock the doors).

quiz.q: Eight ECUs must all be joined point to point. How many links are needed?
A 125 kbit/s body bus carries 30 messages of 110 bits every 50 ms. Find the bus load.
A gateway joins the powertrain bus and the body bus. Give one benefit and one cost of putting them on separate buses instead of one.
quiz.a: Benefit: body traffic and faults cannot load or block the powertrain bus, and the body bus can be slower and cheaper. Cost: messages that cross wait in the gateway, which adds delay and software, and the gateway itself must be diagnosed and protected.

beyond: Not for the exam. Car makers are moving from one ECU per function to a few powerful domain or zone controllers joined by an Ethernet backbone, which shortens the harness further. The gateway also becomes a security border that filters messages from the internet-connected units. Search for zonal E/E architecture and AUTOSAR.
